notes.meaning: Pashhur was an important priest and temple official who was responsible for keeping order. When he heard Jeremiah warn the people about God's coming judgment, he became angry. He used his authority to stop Jeremiah from preaching in the temple courts.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic commentators note that temple officers had a duty to stop false prophets, and Pashhur treated Jeremiah as an impostor.

notes.meaning: Pashhur ordered Jeremiah to be beaten and locked into wooden stocks near a public temple gate. This painful frame forced the prophet into a cramped, twisted position for everyone to see. Faithful messengers of God sometimes face harsh treatment simply for speaking the truth.

The next morning, Pashhur let Jeremiah out of the stocks. Instead of backing down in fear, Jeremiah gave him a new name from the Lord: Magor-missabib, which means 'terror on every side.' This name was a prophecy that fear would soon surround Pashhur wherever he turned.

God warned that Pashhur would become a terrifying sight to himself and his close companions. He would watch his friends die by enemy swords, and the rest of Judah would be carried away by the king of Babylon. His false promises of peace could not protect anyone from God's judgment.

God declared that all the wealth, handcrafted goods, and royal treasures in Jerusalem would be given to their enemies. Invading soldiers from Babylon would strip the city bare and take everything back to their own land. Earthly riches cannot save a nation that turns away from God.

Pashhur and his entire family were sentenced to be taken away to Babylon as prisoners of war. He had told lies to the people, promising them that Jerusalem was safe. Because he misled others, he and his supporters would die and be buried in a foreign land.

Jeremiah poured out his personal agony to God, feeling that the Lord had persuaded him into a task far harder than he imagined. Because he was faithful, people laughed at him and mocked him all day long. God welcomes our honest feelings when ministry and obedience feel overwhelming.

differ.view: Reformed writers explain this either as Jeremiah using holy sarcasm to mirror his enemies' insults, or as a real lapse of human patience under extreme stress.
Baptist commentators see this cry as an honest battle between human weakness and spiritual faith during heavy suffering.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic teachers explain that God did not mislead Jeremiah, but simply did not promise him that serving as a prophet would be free from pain and rejection.

notes.meaning: Whenever Jeremiah spoke, he was required to shout warnings about coming violence and ruin. Because the judgment had not arrived yet, the crowds treated his warnings as a joke. Delivering God's tough messages often brings scorn from those who do not want to change.

Jeremiah tried to resolve within himself to quit preaching so he could escape the constant shame. But God's message became like a roaring fire trapped inside his bones, and he could not hold it in. God's truth has a powerful hold on the hearts of His servants.

Jeremiah heard groups of people whispering and plotting against him, eager to report him to the city leaders. Even his former friends watched for him to stumble so they could get revenge. Following God can sometimes cost us the loyalty of those we once trusted.

Jeremiah found comfort by remembering that the Lord stood beside him like an invincible warrior. Because God was on his side, his persecutors would fail in their traps and face everlasting shame. Remembering God's power gives believers courage when enemies attack.

Jeremiah prayed to the Lord of hosts, who examines the hearts and thoughts of everyone. He asked God to judge his attackers because he had handed his whole situation over to the Lord. Believers can leave their defense in God's hands rather than seeking revenge themselves.

Jeremiah suddenly broke into praise and invited others to sing to the Lord. He rejoiced because God rescues the poor and needy from the power of evil men. Even in hard times, remembering God's past help can fill our hearts with praise.

In deep emotional agony, Jeremiah cursed the day he was born and wished it had received no blessing. His sudden shift back into sorrow shows how hard his inner battle was during this time of persecution.

differ.view: Reformed writers view this bitter outburst as a serious sin of impatience and a failure of faith under extreme trial.
Baptist teaching notes that this complaint shows how even great believers can fall into foolish impatience when crushed by grief.
Methodist commentators suggest these words may recall a past moment of deep despair while Jeremiah sat in the stocks, rather than an immediate change right after his praise.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic tradition reads this verse as poetic speech that highlights the greatness of Jeremiah's suffering rather than actual malice or sin.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Modern scholars see this as a record of Jeremiah's raw personal feelings, closely mirroring the ancient laments found in the book of Job.

notes.meaning: Jeremiah cursed the messenger who ran to tell his father that a baby boy had been born. In that culture, the birth of a son brought great joy, but Jeremiah felt his life had caused only sorrow. Deep grief can make a person wish their happiest moments had never happened.

Jeremiah wished that the messenger had faced total ruin, just like Sodom and Gomorrah, which God destroyed without pity. He wished the man had spent his days hearing the shouts and alarms of invading armies. His words reflect how completely crushed his spirit felt.

Jeremiah wished he had died before taking his first breath, so his mother's womb would have served as his grave. He felt that dying before birth would have been far better than living through such pain. Extreme suffering can tempt people to wish they had never existed.

Jeremiah asked why he was ever born if his life was meant to be filled with endless trouble, sorrow, and shame. Even in his deepest despair, he did not turn away from God, but brought his honest cries directly to Him.
